title: Local Noon Governs the Clock
summary: Before railways and telegraphy, communities commonly set clocks by local solar time, so neighbouring towns could differ by minutes. That variation was manageable when travel and communication were slow. Industrial networks later turned small clock differences into scheduling and safety problems.

title: Franklin Jokes About Saving Morning Light
summary: In a satirical letter written in Paris, Benjamin Franklin calculated that earlier rising could save candle wax and proposed bells and cannon fire to wake sleepers. He did not propose changing clocks or create a daylight-saving programme. Later histories adopted the essay as a witty precursor because it framed daylight as something schedules could waste.

title: Railways Standardise Time
summary: Railways and telegraph networks required common timetables, encouraging railway time and eventually national standard time zones. Once a state could coordinate millions of clocks, it could also move them together by law. Daylight saving was therefore a product of the standardised-time world, not a return to pre-industrial flexibility.

title: George Hudson Proposes a Seasonal Shift
summary: New Zealand entomologist George Vernon Hudson presented a proposal in 1895 to advance clocks seasonally, giving more evening daylight for recreation and collecting insects. His plan is the earliest well-documented modern clock-shifting proposal. It did not immediately become national policy, but it establishes that the idea was not invented by William Willett alone.

title: William Willett Builds a British Campaign
summary: Builder William Willett independently promoted summer time in Britain, proposing four staged twenty-minute advances in spring and reversals in autumn. The familiar story that a morning ride past closed blinds inspired him is family tradition, not the whole explanation. His pamphlet and allies transformed a scheduling idea into a sustained parliamentary campaign, although he died before Britain adopted it.

title: Port Arthur Tries It Locally
summary: Port Arthur, Ontario—now part of Thunder Bay—implemented a local daylight-saving arrangement in 1908, the earliest documented municipal use. It was limited in scale and did not produce a continuous national system. The episode matters because it separates the first local experiment from Germany's later first nationwide adoption.

title: War Makes Clock Policy Attractive
summary: World War I placed fuel, transport, and industrial schedules under intense state control. Governments hoped that shifting civil activity toward evening daylight might reduce demand for artificial lighting, although wartime estimates were uncertain. The emergency supplied the political force that peacetime campaigns had lacked.

title: Germany Moves the Clocks Nationwide
summary: Germany and Austria-Hungary introduced nationwide summer time in 1916 as wartime conservation policy. They were not the first locality ever to try it, but they were the first countries to coordinate it nationally. The measure turned a reform campaign into a policy other belligerents felt pressure to match.

title: Belligerents Follow—Then Reconsider
summary: Britain, France, the United States, and other countries adopted seasonal clock changes during the war or soon after. Many then repealed, suspended, or decentralised the policy when the emergency ended. Daylight saving spread quickly, but acceptance was never universal or irreversible.

title: A Patchwork Replaces Wartime Uniformity
summary: After World War I, national repeal and local choice produced confusing mosaics of observance, particularly in the United States. Cities, counties, transport operators, farmers, and broadcasters had different incentives, so neighbouring places could change clocks on different dates or not at all. The problem was administrative fragmentation rather than a universal public rejection of evening daylight.

title: World War II Brings Year-Round “War Time”
summary: The United States used year-round daylight saving from February 1942 until September 1945, while Britain and other countries adopted their own wartime arrangements, sometimes including double summer time. The policy again rested on conservation and coordination claims rather than precise modern energy measurement. Peacetime systems remained fragmented after the war.

title: The Uniform Time Act Standardises the U.S. Calendar
summary: The U.S. Uniform Time Act of 1966 established common start and end dates for jurisdictions observing daylight saving while allowing states to exempt themselves. It did not make daylight saving permanently year-round, nor did it force every state to participate. Its achievement was replacing a local patchwork with a more coherent national calendar.

title: Arizona Chooses Standard Time
summary: Most of Arizona exempted itself from daylight saving in 1968, preferring not to move an hour of extreme summer heat into the clock-defined evening. The Navajo Nation observes daylight saving, while the Hopi Reservation does not, creating a famous map of nested exceptions. The example shows that latitude, climate, and jurisdiction can matter more than a universal rule.

title: A Temperate-Zone Policy, Not a Global Norm
summary: Seasonal clock changes became common in Europe and parts of North America, but most countries near the equator had little seasonal daylight to reallocate and many other states abandoned the practice. Even among adopters, dates and exemptions differ. Calling DST a global standard conceals how geographically concentrated it remains.

title: The 1974 U.S. Experiment Is Cut Short
summary: The United States began a two-year trial of year-round daylight saving in January 1974 during the oil crisis. Dark winter mornings generated political resistance, and Congress restored standard time for the following winter before the experiment ran its planned course. Federal evaluations found the energy and safety effects too small or uncertain to settle the argument.

title: Energy Savings Depend on Place and Technology
summary: Modern studies do not support one universal energy verdict. A U.S. Department of Energy study of the 2007 extension estimated electricity savings of about 0.02 percent, while research on Indiana found residential electricity use increased by roughly one percent because heating and cooling outweighed lighting savings. Results depend on climate, latitude, behaviour, and the technology being measured.

title: Europe Votes, but the Clocks Keep Changing
summary: After a European Commission consultation drew 4.6 million responses—84 percent favouring an end to seasonal changes—the European Parliament voted in 2019 to discontinue them. The proposal required agreement among member states and the Council, including choices about permanent standard or summer time. As of 2026 that legislative process remains unfinished, so the existing clock changes continue.

title: The Spring Transition Carries a Small Acute Risk
summary: Sleep and cardiovascular studies often find a short-lived increase in adverse events after the spring transition, but effect sizes and methods vary. A recent meta-analysis estimated roughly a four-percent increase in acute myocardial infarction risk after the spring change, not the dramatic figures often repeated in popular summaries. The evidence supports caution about abrupt transitions, not the claim that DST as a whole simply 'kills more people than it saves.'

title: The Argument Is Really About Which Time to Keep
summary: By 2026 the policy debate has split into three questions: whether to keep switching, whether permanent standard time better fits human circadian rhythms, and whether permanent summer time offers social and commercial benefits worth darker mornings. Franklin's satire, wartime conservation, the failed 1974 trial, mixed energy studies, and health evidence are often compressed into slogans. The persistence of DST reflects competing preferences and coordination costs, not the survival of a policy that everyone agrees has failed.
